title: The Guru's script
hookLine: at Khadur, Guru Angad shapes and teaches the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people can read the hymns

lines: THE FIRST TIME YOU READ ALONE.
GURU ANGAD SITS WITH THE CHILDREN.
cards: Remember the first time you read something on your own? A cereal box, a street sign, a picture book. Something clicked, and a world that had belonged to grown-ups belonged to you too.
For most people in the Punjab of the 1500s, that click never came. Reading was for priests, scholars and clerks.
Sacred texts were in Sanskrit, Arabic or Persian, languages ordinary farmers didn't speak, in scripts they couldn't read.

Guru Nanak's hymns, sung in the people's own language, were passed along by memory and in rough notes. Then the new Guru, Angad, moved to a village called Khadur, and there, tradition says, he sat down with the children.

teach.b: The script is called Gurmukhi. Guru is the teacher and mukh is the mouth, so Gurmukhi is often explained as from the mouth of the Guru. The Sikh scripture is written in it, and so is Punjabi across India today.
One careful note: Guru Angad didn't invent writing out of nothing. Scripts much like it were already used in the Punjab, especially by traders keeping accounts.
What Sikh tradition credits him with is shaping those letters into a clear, standard alphabet, putting them in order and teaching them, so anyone could learn to read the Guru's words.

Tradition says he taught the letters to children himself, and helped put together an early primer. On many paths, the holy words sat in a language only specialists could read, so ordinary people needed someone in between.
Guru Angad did the opposite: the hymns in the people's own language, in letters a farmer's child could learn, so the word could go straight from the page into anyone's life.

That's a big part of why Sikhs still treat reading the scripture as something for everyone, man or woman, of any caste. No priestly class holds the book. Anyone who can read Gurmukhi can read the Guru.
Even the first symbol you learned, Ik Onkar, the numeral one and its curve, is written in these letters.

how: Sikh children often learn Gurmukhi at home or in gurdwara classes so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves; any Sikh, of any gender or caste, may read from the scripture.

practice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper, and write your name one letter at a time, slower than you ever do, watching each shape form.
Somebody taught you these letters once; maybe you remember who, a parent at a kitchen table, a teacher in a classroom. Let your pen move slowly enough to remember them.
